captions.text: Project time.
We're building a smart calculator agent: you ask an everyday maths question, and the
agent works it out with real tools, step by step, showing its work.
Everything from the last four lessons comes together here.
We'll take it one file at a time.
Here's what we're building.
You ask a maths question in plain words, at the command line.
The agent has two tools: calculate, for arithmetic, and convert, for units like
kilometres to miles.
It prints every action and every result as it goes.
That printout is called a trace, and it lets you see exactly what the agent did.
And it has a step limit, a budget, clear errors, an offline mode, and a full set of
tests.
Here's the plan.
The command line passes your question to the agent, which runs the loop.
The agent runs tools from tools dot py, and adds up costs with the pricing module
from Module 2.
And it talks to the model through the client: the real Claude API with a key, or the
offline fake without one.
First, a word about the offline fake, so you know exactly what you're seeing in this
video.
It speaks the same protocol as the real API, so the SDK and our loop run unchanged.
But it follows a fixed script: it finds arithmetic and unit conversions in the
question, asks for one tool per turn, then writes a placeholder answer.
That's not a model.
It can't understand a word problem, it can't plan, and it can't check its work.
No API key was used in this recording, so every model turn you see comes from this
script.
The tools and the loop, though, are completely real.
You've seen calculate.
The second tool is convert.
It uses one table: each unit has a kind, like length or mass, and a factor that
converts it to a base unit.
For example, one kilometre is a thousand metres.
Temperatures are different: Celsius to Fahrenheit needs a formula, not a simple
factor, so they get their own small branch.
An unknown unit, or converting kilograms to kilometres, raises a tool error with a
helpful message, which goes back to the model as an observation.
And the conversion itself is one line: multiply by one factor, divide by the other.
When the model asks for a tool, run tool connects the name to the right Python
function.
This is called dispatching.
For convert, it also checks the inputs.
If anything is missing or the wrong type, the model gets a clear message saying what
was expected.
And if the model asks for a tool that doesn't exist, it's refused.
The agent can only use the tools you chose to give it.
Now the agent itself.
A step records one action and what was observed: the tool, its input, its output,
and whether it was an error.
A result holds the answer, and, just as important, why the loop stopped: answered,
max steps, refused, cut off, or budget.
It also keeps the steps, the number of turns, and the cost.
Decide sends one request: the instructions, the tools, low effort because these are
simple decisions, and the whole message list.
Then it records the cost of that request, and returns the reply.
And here's run.
It's the same loop as lesson three, with all the safety from lesson four.
It runs at most max steps turns, and checks the budget before every turn.
Decide, store the reply unchanged, then stop cleanly on a refusal or a cut-off
reply.
No tool requests means we have the answer.
Otherwise we act, report each step so the trace can print it, and send back the
results, including the is error flag.
And if the loop runs out of turns, we stop with max steps.
First, the calc command runs the calculator tool directly, with no model at all.
It's useful for checking that a tool works on its own.
And now the agent.
One act, one observe, and an answer, in two turns.
The footer shows the turns, the tool calls, and the cost, which is an estimate
offline.
Pause and think it through, using the run tool code you saw.
One.
The model asks for a tool called delete files.
What happens?
Two.
It calls convert, with the value lots.
What happens?
One: run tool raises a tool error, unknown tool, which goes back to the model as an
observation.
Nothing is deleted, because that tool simply doesn't exist in our program.
Two: turning lots into a number fails, so the model gets a clear message saying
convert needs a value, a from unit, and a to unit.
We built two tools with clear errors: calculate and convert.
Run tool dispatches by name, and refuses unknown tools.
And the loop records every step, and exactly why it stopped.
